comments.author: Prox1mus
comments.body:
When i look at vibe-coded games, the first thing I look at is the UI/UX …because it sticks out immediately for me. Almost every vibe-coded project shares that same distinctive GPT/Claude interface style. Why? Because most vibe-coders lack a background in UX design or visual hierarchy and offload the entire aesthetic burden onto the LLM. And don't get me wrong, I get why its so tempting to focus on the main assets first. But fonts, layout and ui architecture basically define how a game actually *feels*.

The result is super predictable… without a specific prompt directing its aesthetic strategy, the AI simply solves the functional task. This yields the exact same template every single time: rounded HUD panels, semi-transparent glassmorphism and a few subtle glows. If you don't have a design background, it's hard to pinpoint why this feels off—because at first glance it looks sleek, right?

It doesn't. But your LLM won't break that news to you. Breaking out of this default trap requires basic knowledge of visual hierarchy, proportions and layout logic – which is precisely where exceptional vibe-coded games set themselves apart. The good part is even if you have no knowledge about a specific topic you just have to understand the basic principles of it to ask and trigger the right response of the llm. 

What is rarely realised is that the barrier isn't tech, its communication. Most users hold a vivid vision in their head but lack the technical vocabulary to articulate it. TLDR: Faced with ambiguity, the LLM just fills the gaps with its statistical average of a web UI.

comments.body: I really like the way you've rendered the rocks. I'm making a planet exploration game, but rendering the rocks and the surface is difficult... Do you have any tips?

replies.author: ykosyakov
replies.body:
The asteroid is one smooth mesh, and a single shader paints each pixel with the texture of whatever it's made of: dust, stone, ice, gold, crystal. Those textures are procedural tiles baked in Blender and projected from three sides, so no UVs are needed. On top of that the shader adds small craters with their own shadows, pale dust on flat ground and pebbles on slopes, and lighter rock wherever you've dug. Real 3D boulders and half-buried ore crystals are scattered over it, dusted at the base so they look settled in.

  
DM if get more questions
